_about: Category changes make-seed.py applies on top of the dashboard repo's programs.json. remove drops categories by folder; drop leaves programs out by id, wherever they come from (68 Socio-Economic, Nov. 12, 2026); add appends programs to kept categories, by folder; their programs are placed again under the new categories by id. A program entry is one of: {id} for a program from programs.json or LT Info (name overrides the LT Info name); {id, indicator} for a threshold indicator with no monitoring program, built from its Threshold Dashboard record, id 9600 plus its threshold indicator id; or {id, ltinfo: false, ...} written here, with description and approach as lists of paragraphs. Category ids from 11. relatedIndicators on an entry, and related (program id to LT Info indicator ids) for programs from programs.json, name the LT Info indicators whose pages on the other dashboards the program links to, besides the ones LT Info links it to. organizations gives short names for partners LT Info does not have. icon is a path in Sandbox.Web/public for categories the Threshold Dashboard has no icon for.
_sources: Forest Structure and Fire Dynamics: the Forest Health Threshold Standards Update story map collection (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/collections/d89adce0aa9047efb018e49a6f8eff87) for the standards and their background, and the monitoring approach sections of the ForestHealth repo's monitoring/forest-structure.html and monitoring/fire-dynamics.html. Biodiversity's goal joins the adopted Threshold Dashboard descriptions of the three categories it replaces (Vegetation Preservation, Fisheries, and Wildlife). Indicator pages: the Threshold Dashboard records at internalapi.laketahoeinfo.org/threshold-indicators/{id}. Added programs: the LT Info monitoring programs not in programs.json that have a monitoring approach, partners, and usually threshold indicators, reviewed Nov. 11, 2026. Left out: 67 Air Quality (umbrella of the five pollutant programs), 37 Infrastructure (empty), 75 bike ped test, 80 Effective Population (one line), 28 East Shore Parking Counts (no partners or indicators), and 31 Nearshore Resource Allocation Program (coordination umbrella). Demographics: the Tahoe Open Data demographics page (https://www.tahoeopendata.org/pages/demographics) for the text, its figures for the age, race, occupancy, and county income charts, and the Demographics map service (Demographic Summaries table and community change layer) for the rest. Affordable and Workforce Housing: TRPA Long Range Planning's parcel inventory, read from the copy behind the Housing Progress page (https://trpa-agency.github.io/Planning/LongRange/html/multifamily-housing.html) by tools/extract-housing-inventory.py. SMART Traffic Cameras: the Transportation_SMART feature service and the README, config.yaml, and metadata/field_descriptions.yaml of the SMART_Phase1 folder in TRPA's Transportation repository on GitHub (https://github.com/trpa-agency/Transportation/tree/main/SMART_Phase1) for how the data is collected and loaded, and for the event names.

transportation-and-sustainable-communiti.name: SMART Traffic Cameras
description: Fifteen cameras at highway intersections and recreation sites around the Tahoe Basin count vehicles and people walking and biking, and log near misses and other safety events, using computer vision. Thirteen are permanent, and two were temporary.

The Tahoe Transportation District installed the cameras under a U.S. Department of Transportation SMART grant (Strengthening Mobility and Revolutionizing Transportation), with TRPA as the data partner. The record starts in March 2025.
approach: Derq's computer vision software reads each camera's video. It classifies what passes (passenger vehicles, trucks, buses, motorcycles, bicycles, and people walking) and counts them in 15-minute intervals by direction of approach. It also logs one record for each safety event, such as a near miss, wrong-way driving, or an illegal crossing.

A TRPA script pulls the counts and events from Derq and loads them to the Transportation_SMART feature service on maps.trpa.org, replacing each day in full so that a rerun never duplicates records. Daily totals are the sum of the 15-minute vehicle counts.

Read the totals with care. The cameras were switched on at different times, so a total is not comparable between cameras without allowing for the days each one counted. The speed table is one distribution for the whole Phase 1 record and is no longer updated. Three event names (lane change violation, turn violation, and stopped vehicle) are TRPA's reading of Derq's codes and are not yet confirmed with Derq.

categories.name: Forest Structure
categories.blurb: Seral stage, canopy cover, and stand density of the conifer forest.
categories.goal: Restore a balanced mosaic of forest ages, from young trees to old growth, and of open and closed canopies, and keep stands at densities that leave forests less vulnerable to drought, insects, disease, and severe wildfire.

programs.name: Seral Stage and Canopy Cover
description: Seral stage is the developmental phase of a forest, from young regeneration to mature stands of large trees. Canopy cover is the share of the forest floor shaded by tree crowns, from open to closed. Together they shape how a forest grows and changes, and the wildlife and ecosystems it can support.

More than a century ago, natural fire kept a mosaic of early, mid, and late seral stands across the Tahoe Basin, with a balance of open and closed canopies. Clear-cutting in the Comstock era, followed by more than 100 years of fire suppression and past management, left many stands dense, uniform, and heavy with fuel. Dense, middle-aged forest is overrepresented today.

The Seral Stage and Canopy Cover threshold standard calls for at least 75 percent of forested acres to fall within desired ranges for seral stage and canopy cover. The ranges are set for each of three forest types, Jeffrey pine, Sierra mixed conifer, and red fir, and reflect conditions that support resilience, habitat diversity, and fire-adapted forest structure.
Meeting the ranges takes both active management, such as thinning and beneficial fire to open up canopies, and protection that lets existing stands mature into late seral forest.
approach: Seral stage and canopy cover are mapped across the conifer forest from the Sierra Nevada Regional Resource Kit, 30-meter remote sensing products, in the 2023 assessment as published to the TRPA Vegetation service. Seral stage follows quadratic mean diameter: early under 5 inches, mid 5 to 25 inches, and late over 25 inches. Closed canopy is 40 percent cover or more in Jeffrey pine, and 50 percent or more in Sierra mixed conifer and red fir.
Each forest type's acres are compared with its desired share in five classes: early seral, mid seral open, mid seral closed, late seral open, and late seral closed.
Jeffrey pine: early 5 to 15 percent, mid open 25 to 30 percent, mid closed 5 to 10 percent, late open 40 to 50 percent, and late closed 5 to 10 percent.
Sierra mixed conifer: early 10 to 20 percent, mid open 15 to 20 percent, mid closed 5 to 15 percent, late open 25 to 35 percent, and late closed 15 to 25 percent.
Red fir: early 10 to 20 percent, mid open 15 to 25 percent, mid closed 15 to 25 percent, late open 30 to 40 percent, and late closed 20 to 30 percent.

measures.title: Conifer forest acres by seral stage and canopy cover
measures.sub: Acres of conifer forest in each seral stage and canopy class, 2023 assessment.

programs.name: Stand Density
description: Stand density measures how many trees grow in an area (trees per acre) and the total cross-section of their trunks (basal area, in square feet per acre).

After a century of fire suppression, Tahoe's forests are far denser than they were historically. Crowded trees compete for water, nutrients, and sunlight, and stressed trees are more vulnerable to drought, insects, and disease. Recent droughts have raised mortality: the USDA Forest Service aerial detection survey recorded more than 1.7 million dead trees across 66,000 acres of the Tahoe Basin in 2023.

The Stand Density threshold standard calls for at least 50 percent of forested area to fall within recommended ranges of trees per acre and basal area for its forest type and seral stage. Thinning overcrowded stands reduces competition among trees and improves their resilience to drought and wildfire.
approach: Trees per acre and basal area are mapped across the conifer forest from the Sierra Nevada Regional Resource Kit, 30-meter remote sensing products, in the 2023 assessment as published to the TRPA Vegetation service, and tested together against the recommended maximum for each forest type and seral stage. An acre at or below both values is within range.
Jeffrey pine: early seral 200 trees and 30 square feet of basal area per acre, mid seral 70 trees and 80 square feet, and late seral 55 trees and 100 square feet.
Sierra mixed conifer: early seral 300 trees and 40 square feet, mid seral 90 trees and 130 square feet, and late seral 75 trees and 180 square feet.
Red fir: early seral 300 trees and 50 square feet, mid seral 100 trees and 175 square feet, and late seral 80 trees and 250 square feet.

measures.title: Conifer forest acres within the recommended density
measures.sub: Acres at or below the recommended trees per acre and basal area for their forest type and seral stage, and acres over it, 2023 assessment.

programs.name: Large Trees
description: Large trees, more than 36 inches in diameter at breast height, are the backbone of an old forest. They store the most carbon, survive low-intensity fire behind thick bark, and give nesting and denning sites to wildlife such as the California spotted owl, northern goshawk, and Pacific marten.

Comstock-era logging cut most of the Basin's large trees in the late 1800s. The trees that escaped it, and the forest that has grown since, set how much old forest structure the Basin has today. Counting large trees over time shows whether that structure is recovering or being lost to drought, insects, and severe fire.
approach: Individual trees were mapped across the Basin from airborne LiDAR flown in 2010, with each tree's diameter estimated from its LiDAR measurements. The layer holds the 84,373 trees estimated at more than 36 inches.
The map counts the trees in hexagons of 100 acres each. The count will be repeated with the next Basin-wide LiDAR flight, so the change in large trees can be measured.

programs.name: Tree Mortality
description: Tree mortality is the forest dying faster than it grows back. Drought weakens trees, and bark beetles and other insects kill the weakened ones, often across whole hillsides. Dense stands, where trees compete for water, are hit hardest.

The 2023 survey found fir engraver beetles killing California red fir across the Basin's upper slopes, with Jeffrey pine beetle and mountain pine beetle in smaller patches. Dead trees add to the fuel that can carry severe fire, which ties tree mortality to both stand density and fire dynamics.
approach: The USDA Forest Service aerial detection survey is flown over California's forests each summer. Surveyors sketch each area of recent damage from the air and record the host tree, the agent that killed it, the share of trees affected, and an estimate of trees killed.

This page reads the 2023 survey: the damage areas within or touching the TRPA boundary. Areas that cross the boundary are counted whole, so the totals run higher than the Basin alone. Each year's survey added to the service builds the trend.

categories.name: Fire Dynamics
categories.blurb: Burn probability, likely fire severity, and area burned.
categories.goal: Keep fire behavior defensible around neighborhoods and evacuation routes, and limit the size and extent of large, high-severity fire patches across the forested landscape.

programs.name: Annual Burn Probability
description: Annual burn probability is the chance that a given spot in the Basin burns in any one year. It comes from simulating thousands of fire seasons over the Basin's own fuels, weather, topography, and history of ignitions, and counting how often each 30-meter cell burns.

Burn probability is the likelihood half of wildfire hazard; likely fire severity is the intensity half. Together they show where fire is most likely to come and how hard it would burn. Fuel treatments lower both over time.
approach: Vibrant Planet's Quantitative Wildfire Risk Assessment for the Lake Tahoe Basin models annual and 10-year burn probability with the FSim fire simulator, on fuels updated for disturbance and regrowth through the end of 2025. It replaces the 2022 CAL FIRE modeling the Region uses now, which reflects fuels through 2021.
Burn probability will be reported as the share of each forest management zone in each probability class, and repeated with each model update.

programs.name: Likely Fire Severity
description: Fire has long shaped Sierra Nevada forests. Frequent, low-intensity fire every decade or two at Tahoe's lower elevations kept fuels in check and forests open and diverse. A century of fire suppression has let fuels build up and forests become overstocked, raising the risk of large, high-severity fires that burn hotter, are harder to control, and can damage soils, wildlife habitat, communities, and infrastructure.

Likely fire severity is the outcome a fire would most likely have in each part of the forest under hot, dry, windy weather: low, moderate, or high severity. Low-severity fire clears brush and small trees and leaves most large trees alive. High-severity fire kills most trees, and large high-severity patches leave few surviving trees to reseed the forest.

Two threshold standards read it. The WUI Defense Zone standard calls for at least 90 percent of the Defense Zone, the land right around homes and roads, to have predicted flame lengths of four feet or less, the limit at which firefighters can safely attack a fire directly. The Landscape standard limits modeled high-severity patches of 200 acres or more to less than 5 percent of the forested landscape.
In the 2021 Caldor Fire, many treated areas burned at low severity, but nearly 5,000 acres burned at high severity in large patches, closely matching what the modeling predicted.
approach: Fire severity is modeled across the Basin under 90th percentile fire weather with the Pyrologix Wildfire Exposure Simulation Tool, delivered through the Sierra Nevada Regional Resource Kit. Each 30-meter cell gets its most likely severity, low, moderate, or high, summarized here by forest management zone.

Low severity stands in for flame lengths of four feet or less. Vibrant Planet's Quantitative Wildfire Risk Assessment will replace this run with flame length at the 90th, 95th, and 97th percentile of fire weather, on fuels updated through 2025.

measures.title: Most likely fire severity by management zone
measures.sub: Acres of each forest management zone by most likely fire severity under 90th percentile fire weather.

measures.title: WUI Defense Zone by most likely fire severity
measures.sub: Acres of the mapped WUI Defense Zone, urban footprint included, by most likely fire severity. Low severity stands in for flame lengths of four feet or less.

measures.title: Most likely high severity fire by management zone
measures.sub: Acres where high severity is the most likely outcome, all patch sizes. The Landscape standard counts only patches of 200 acres or more.

programs.name: Area Burned
description: Area burned is the acres of wildfire inside the Basin each year. It is the observed record that the modeled measures, burn probability and likely fire severity, are checked against.

For most of the last century the Basin saw few large fires, a result of fire suppression rather than of a forest that does not burn. The 2007 Angora Fire burned about 3,100 acres and 254 homes near South Lake Tahoe. The 2021 Caldor Fire burned about 9,900 acres inside the Basin, the largest fire in the record here, before firefighters stopped it in treated forest near Meyers.
approach: Fire perimeters come from CAL FIRE's statewide fire history, which maps fires on the California side of the Basin; Nevada fires and many small fires are not in it. Each perimeter is clipped to the TRPA boundary and measured in California Albers, so a fire that started outside the Basin counts only the acres that burned inside it.
The Tahoe Fire and Fuels Team fire history, 1988 to 2025, covers both states and will replace this record once it is published.

categories.name: Demographics
categories.blurb: Population, age, race and ethnicity, housing, and income of the Tahoe Region.
categories.goal: Describe who lives in the Tahoe Region and how that is changing, from census counts and estimates, to inform housing, transportation, and community planning.

programs.name: Population
description: The Lake Tahoe Region had 55,836 residents at the 2020 census. Population peaked at 62,843 in 2000; over the 30 years from 1990 to 2020 it grew 6 percent, while the five surrounding counties grew 92 percent, Nevada 138 percent, and California 33 percent.

In 2020, 72 percent of the Region's residents lived in the California portion of the Basin and 28 percent in Nevada, and 64 percent lived in south shore communities. California communities declined 2 percent from 2010 to 2020 and are 12 percent below the 2000 peak, while Nevada communities grew 7 percent.

Incline Village and Crystal Bay grew fastest from 2010 to 2020, up 8 percent. Homewood fell 9 percent and Tahoma 7 percent. The City of South Lake Tahoe declined 2 percent, and Meyers grew 3 percent. The Placer County communities on the north and west shores declined 4 percent from 2010 and are 17 percent below the 2000 peak; only Lake Forest and Dollar Hill grew, up 3 percent.
approach: Figures come from the U.S. Census Bureau's decennial census and American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, queried through the Census Bureau's API and summarized for the Tahoe Region by TRPA. Decennial counts are a full count every 10 years; ACS estimates are yearly averages of five years of samples, so they move more smoothly and carry a margin of error.

In 2020 the census boundaries changed. The Lake Tahoe Region is made up of 31 census tracts and 78 block groups along the California and Nevada border. The Carson City tract straddles the TRPA boundary with most of its people outside it, so it is left out.
The tables and boundaries are on the TRPA Demographics map service, and the code behind the figures is in TRPA's Demographics repository on GitHub.

measures.sub: Residents of the Lake Tahoe Region counted in each decennial census.

programs.name: Age
description: The Basin's residents have grown older over three decades and are now slightly older than those of nearby counties and urban areas. The baby boom generation shows in the age profile: the largest age group was 30 to 40 in 1990, 40 to 50 in 2000, and 60 to 70 by 2020.

Millennials form a second peak, at ages 25 to 40, that the surrounding five counties do not show, perhaps because of the Region's appeal to people seeking an active outdoor life. One resident in five was 65 or older in 2020, up from fewer than one in 10 in 1990.
approach: Figures come from the U.S. Census Bureau's decennial census and American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, queried through the Census Bureau's API and summarized for the Tahoe Region by TRPA. Decennial counts are a full count every 10 years; ACS estimates are yearly averages of five years of samples, so they move more smoothly and carry a margin of error.

In 2020 the census boundaries changed. The Lake Tahoe Region is made up of 31 census tracts and 78 block groups along the California and Nevada border. The Carson City tract straddles the TRPA boundary with most of its people outside it, so it is left out.
The tables and boundaries are on the TRPA Demographics map service, and the code behind the figures is in TRPA's Demographics repository on GitHub.

programs.name: Race and Ethnicity
description: The Basin's population has grown more diverse since the 2000 census. The share of residents who identify as Hispanic or Latino rose from 18 percent in 2000 to 22 percent in 2020, and Black, Indigenous, and other people of color made up about 31 percent of residents in 2020, up from 24 percent in 2000.

Decennial counts are a full count every 10 years; ACS estimates are yearly averages of five years of samples, so they move more smoothly and carry a margin of error.

The race map places one dot for every 25 people at random within each census tract, from the American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2019 to 2023 (Esri's ACS Population by Race and Hispanic Origin layer, the one the Tahoe Open Data map uses). Dots show how many people live in each tract, not where in the tract they live, and tracts on the Basin's edge reach past the TRPA boundary.

categories.name: Climate and Lake Conditions
categories.blurb: Greenhouse gas emissions, smoke, lake level and temperature, precipitation, and renewable energy.
categories.goal: Track how a changing climate is reaching the Tahoe Region, from smoke days and a warmer lake to less snow, and the Region's progress cutting the emissions that drive it.

programs.name: Greenhouse Gas Emissions
description: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat in the atmosphere and drive climate change. In the Tahoe Region most emissions come from heating and powering buildings and from driving.
The Region set a goal of cutting emissions 15 percent below 2005 levels by 2020, which it met, and of reaching net zero by 2045.
approach: TRPA inventories the Region's greenhouse gas emissions every few years from energy use, fuel sales, vehicle miles traveled, solid waste, and wastewater, following the U.S. Community Protocol. Emissions are reported in metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent.

measures.title: Greenhouse gas emissions by sector
measures.sub: Metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in each inventory year.

programs.name: Air Quality and Wildfire Smoke
description: Wildfire smoke now brings the Tahoe Region its worst air of the year. Fine particles in smoke reach deep into the lungs, and smoke days are expected to grow as fire seasons lengthen.
approach: A network of low-cost PurpleAir sensors around the Basin measures fine particulate matter (PM2.5) continuously. Readings from sensors that pass quality checks are averaged each day and converted to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Air Quality Index. Values above 100 are unhealthy for sensitive groups.

measures.title: Daily air quality index
measures.sub: Daily mean Air Quality Index from PurpleAir sensors in the Basin, 2017 to 2024.

programs.name: Lake Level
description: Lake Tahoe's surface rises with snowmelt and falls through dry years. Below the natural rim, 6,223 feet, no water flows out into the Truckee River. Above it, the dam at Tahoe City holds the lake no higher than the legal limit of 6,229.1 feet.
A warmer climate shifts precipitation from snow to rain and lengthens droughts, which makes the swings between full and low lake more extreme.
approach: The U.S. Geological Survey gauges the lake level at Tahoe City. The chart shows the weekly mean against the natural rim and the legal limit.

measures.title: Lake Tahoe water level
measures.sub: Weekly mean elevation of the lake surface, feet above sea level, 2007 to 2025.

programs.name: Lake Surface Temperature
description: Lake Tahoe's surface water has warmed over the last half century. Warmer water mixes less often, holds less oxygen at depth, and favors algae and warm-water invasive species.
approach: A buoy at mid-lake records the surface temperature through the year. The chart shows the daily mean in degrees Fahrenheit for the most recent year published.

measures.title: Mid-lake surface temperature
measures.sub: Daily mean surface temperature at mid-lake, degrees Fahrenheit, January 2024 to January 2025.

programs.name: Precipitation and Snow
partners: UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Laboratory
description: Most of the Tahoe Region's water arrives as winter snow, which melts slowly into streams and the lake through spring and summer. As the climate warms, more of it falls as rain, runs off sooner, and leaves less snowpack for the dry season.
approach: The Central Sierra Snow Laboratory near Donner Pass, just outside the Basin, has a daily record of precipitation and snowfall from 1970. Totals here are by calendar year. The share falling as snow comes from the same record.

measures.title: Share of precipitation as snow and rain
measures.sub: Percent of each year's precipitation that fell as snow and as rain, 1987 to 2019.

measures.title: Total precipitation
measures.sub: Millimeters of precipitation, rain and the water in snow, by calendar year, 1970 to 2019.

measures.title: New snowfall
measures.sub: Centimeters of new snow, by calendar year, 1970 to 2019.

programs.name: Renewable Energy
description: Electricity generation is one of the Region's largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions. Shifting the power supply to solar, wind, geothermal, and hydropower lowers emissions without asking residents to use less.
approach: Liberty Utilities serves the California side of the Basin and NV Energy the Nevada side. Each reports the share of its power mix from renewable sources each year.

measures.title: Electricity from renewable sources
measures.sub: Share of each utility's power mix from renewable and non-renewable sources.

categories.name: Housing and Economy
categories.blurb: Housing, deed-restricted homes, prices and rents, jobs, income, and the visitor economy.
categories.goal: Track whether people who work in the Region can afford to live here, and how resilient the Region's economy is.

programs.name: Housing
description: Over four decades, homes occupied by full-time residents have held at slightly under half of all housing in the Basin, except in 2000, when they rose to 55 percent. Seasonal, recreational, or occasional use accounted for almost half of all housing in 2020.
The Basin had 49,592 housing units at the 2020 census, of which 21,883 were seasonal homes, up from 12,757 in 1990.
approach: Figures come from the U.S. Census Bureau's decennial census and American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, queried through the Census Bureau's API and summarized for the Tahoe Region by TRPA. Decennial counts are a full count every 10 years; ACS estimates are yearly averages of five years of samples, so they move more smoothly and carry a margin of error.

In 2020 the census boundaries changed. The Lake Tahoe Region is made up of 31 census tracts and 78 block groups along the California and Nevada border. The Carson City tract straddles the TRPA boundary with most of its people outside it, so it is left out.
The tables and boundaries are on the TRPA Demographics map service, and the code behind the figures is in TRPA's Demographics repository on GitHub.

programs.name: Income
description: Household incomes in the Basin have generally risen over the past decade, with a notable rise from 2019 to 2021, the latest years with census estimates. In the Washoe County part of the Basin, median income adjusted for inflation rose 29 percent from 2019 to 2021, while elsewhere in the Basin it held roughly steady.
approach: Figures come from the U.S. Census Bureau's decennial census and American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, queried through the Census Bureau's API and summarized for the Tahoe Region by TRPA. Decennial counts are a full count every 10 years; ACS estimates are yearly averages of five years of samples, so they move more smoothly and carry a margin of error.

In 2020 the census boundaries changed. The Lake Tahoe Region is made up of 31 census tracts and 78 block groups along the California and Nevada border. The Carson City tract straddles the TRPA boundary with most of its people outside it, so it is left out.

measures.sub: Median household income in each county's part of the Basin, 2021 dollars.

programs.name: Deed-Restricted Housing
description: A deed restriction keeps a home affordable, or reserved for people who work in the Region, for as long as the restriction is recorded. TRPA grants development bonuses and other incentives for housing that carries one.
Restrictions come in three income levels: affordable, for households earning up to 80 percent of area median income; moderate, up to 120 percent; and achievable, for local workers at any income.
approach: TRPA records each deed restriction with its parcel, type, and number of units, and maps the parcels that carry one.

measures.title: Deed-restricted units by type
measures.sub: Housing units with a recorded deed restriction, by income level.

programs.name: Home Prices and Rents
description: Home prices in the Tahoe Region have risen far faster than local wages, and many homes sell as second homes or vacation rentals. The gap pushes people who work here to live outside the Basin and commute in.
approach: Home sale prices are the average of each month's mean residential sale price in the Basin. Rents are the asking rent per unit in multifamily buildings, by quarter, from a commercial rental market survey.

measures.title: Average home sale price
measures.sub: Mean of the monthly average residential sale price, by year, dollars.

measures.title: Asking rent per unit
measures.sub: Average monthly asking rent per multifamily unit, by quarter, dollars.

programs.name: Transient Occupancy Tax
description: Transient occupancy tax is charged on hotel, motel, and short-term rental stays. Its revenue tracks the visitor economy the Region depends on, and how it shifts with snow years, fire seasons, and the economy.
approach: Each local jurisdiction reports the tax collected in each fiscal year, July through June. El Dorado County's collections are not in the fiscal-year record, so the totals cover the other four jurisdictions.

measures.title: Transient occupancy tax collected
measures.sub: Dollars collected each fiscal year, by jurisdiction.

programs.name: Jobs and Wages
description: Steady, well-paid jobs let people who work in the Region afford to live here. Tahoe's economy leans on seasonal tourism and recreation, which keeps many jobs part-year and many wages low.
approach: The U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program counts jobs by work location each year from unemployment insurance records, in three monthly earnings bands. The 2022 count is about double 2021, which looks like a processing error, so the chart ends at 2021.

measures.title: Jobs in the Basin by monthly earnings
measures.sub: Jobs located in the Basin each year, by monthly earnings band, 2002 to 2021.

programs.name: Affordable and Workforce Housing
description: TRPA's inventory of affordable and workforce housing counts 8,582 existing homes in the Tahoe Region as of Sept. 23, 2026: apartments and other multifamily buildings, mobile homes, single room occupancy units, deed-restricted homes, and accessory dwelling units. Two thirds are in the City of South Lake Tahoe.

Another 654 units are in the pipeline: 571 permitted but not yet built, and 83 bonus units reserved for projects that have not applied. About 400 units have been built since the 2012 Regional Plan, more than half of them deed-restricted, with the largest additions in 2024 and 2025.
approach: TRPA Long Range Planning keeps the inventory as a list of parcels. Each record has the jurisdiction, number of units, year built, housing type, and status: built before 2012, built 2012 or later, permitted but not built, or bonus units reserved.

The housing type on a record names either the building form or the deed restriction, and some records name two. The charts count a record as an accessory dwelling unit first, then as deed-restricted, then by its building form.

The inventory is a spreadsheet and is not yet published as a map service, so these charts read a copy taken from TRPA's Housing Progress page. Its deed-restricted counts come from a different list than the Deed-Restricted Housing page, and the two do not match.

measures.title: Units by jurisdiction and status
measures.sub: Affordable and workforce housing units in each jurisdiction: built, permitted, and reserved.

measures.title: Units built each year since 2012
measures.sub: Existing units by year built, since the 2012 Regional Plan. 2026 is a partial year.

measures.title: Existing units by housing type
measures.sub: Existing units by the type on each record. Accessory dwelling units are counted first, then deed-restricted homes.
